walkthroughs.body_html:
Probability — a core area of A-Level Maths.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Probability brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Probability.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: If P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5, and A, B are independent, P(A ∩ B) =:
P(A ∪ B) where P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.5, P(A ∩ B) = 0.1 is:
If you've flipped a fair coin and got heads 5 times in a row, what is the probability the next flip is heads?
options: Less than 1/2, because the coin is 'due' to land on tails to balance the results.
1/2 — each flip is independent of the previous ones.
P(A | B) is always P(A) + P(B).
1 because the coin has clearly been biased by the previous flips.

mcqs.q: Is P(A | B) the same as P(B | A)?
options: 1 because the coin has clearly been biased by the previous flips.
P(A | B) is always P(A) + P(B).
P(A | B) = P(B | A) because conditioning is symmetric.
Generally no — these conditional probabilities are different unless P(A) = P(B).
5.33, by dividing 80 by 15.
15, because 15% means 15 units out of any amount.
P(A | B) is always P(A) + P(B).
